input: Safety stock plays a crucial role in ensuring that service levels are maintained in the face of variable demand, and it is therefore important to set the level in a careful and systematic manner. For the packaging film considered here, the relevant parameters are as follows: mean demand amounts to 3994 units per week, the standard deviation of weekly demand is 925 units per week, and the replenishment lead time is 6 weeks. On the basis of these parameters, and targeting a 95% cycle service level, the safety stock is set at 3739 units. In other words, holding 3739 units of safety stock is intended to ensure that demand fluctuations arising during the lead time can be accommodated in the great majority of replenishment cycles. It should be noted that this calculation rests on a number of important assumptions: demand is treated as normally distributed, demand from week to week is treated as independent, and seasonal peaks are excluded from the analysis. As a result, if a seasonal peak were to occur within a lead time, the safety stock might prove insufficient, and stockouts could occur despite the buffer that has been put in place. Overall, the figure provides a useful and practical basis for the inventory policy, provided that the underlying assumptions continue to hold for the film in question.
target: Set the safety stock for the packaging film at 3739 units. Mean demand is 3994 units per week, with a standard deviation of 925 units per week, and the replenishment lead time is 6 weeks. At a 95% cycle service level, the safety stock of 3739 units covers demand variation over the lead time at the stated service level. Cycle service level denotes the share of replenishment cycles that close without a stockout. The calculation treats demand as normal and as independent between weeks. Demand in one week carries no information about demand in the next week under the independence assumption, so variation builds across the lead time instead of cancelling. Seasonal peaks are excluded from the demand record, so the figure does not cover a seasonal peak that falls inside a lead time. A week of demand above the mean draws on the safety stock first; the stock is sized to the spread of weekly demand, not to the mean. The mean demand sets the cycle stock; the safety stock stands on top of the cycle stock and is untouched in an average week. If the lead time lengthens or the weekly spread widens, the same service level requires a larger stock, and the policy figure has to be recomputed from the new values.
